moments.title: Arithmetic and geometric patterns
moments.text: Arithmetic sequences have a common difference; geometric sequences have a common ratio.

moments.title: Term labels
moments.text: $u_1$, $u_2$ and $u_3$ denote the first three terms; $u_n$ denotes term $n$.

moments.title: A negative ratio
moments.text: For $5,-25,125,-625,\ldots$, divide a term by the preceding nonzero term to find $r=-5$.

moments.title: Alternating signs
moments.text: A negative ratio changes the sign at each multiplication when the terms are nonzero.

moments.title: A ratio between zero and one
moments.text: In $100,50,25,12.5,\ldots$, each term is half its predecessor, so $r=1/2$.

moments.title: A negative fractional ratio
moments.text: The sequence $27,-9,3,-1,\ldots$ has $r=-1/3$: signs alternate and magnitudes decrease.

moments.title: Formulas for geometric sequences
moments.text: The presenter identifies the formulas for terms and sums and separates the higher-level infinite-sum formula.

moments.title: Find the eighth term
moments.text: For $u_1=2$ and $r=2$, substitute into $u_n=u_1r^{n-1}$ to obtain $u_8=256$.

moments.title: From terms to a series
moments.text: The next task adds terms rather than finding one term: $S_n$ is the sum of the first $n$ terms.

moments.title: Two equivalent finite-sum formulas
moments.text: For $r\ne1$, $u_1(r^n-1)/(r-1)$ and $u_1(1-r^n)/(1-r)$ give the same sum.

moments.title: An infinite geometric series
moments.text: The video introduces the infinite sum and contrasts shrinking terms with the increasing example.

moments.title: Successive partial sums
moments.text: For a convergent series, adding more terms can bring the partial sum increasingly close to a finite limit; it does not generally become exactly equal to the limit.

notes.title: Condition for an infinite sum
notes.text: The video describes the condition as the common ratio being less than 1. That alone also includes ratios such as $-2$, which do not give a convergent nonzero geometric series.
notes.write: The infinite geometric series converges when $|r|<1$, or equivalently $-1<r<1$. Then $S_\infty=u_1/(1-r)$.

notes.title: Exact limit versus rounded values
notes.text: The presenter says successive partial sums eventually stay the same. They can appear equal after rounding while still changing.
notes.write: For $|r|<1$, the infinite sum is the exact limit of the partial sums; a finite partial sum is generally an approximation to it.

ican.text: I can determine the common ratio and decide whether an infinite geometric series converges.
I can calculate an infinite sum when the convergence condition is met.
I can compare a finite partial sum with the infinite limit and find the remaining sum.
I can model a repeated process, such as rebounds, using an infinite geometric series and interpret the result.
I can distinguish an infinite series from a sequence of its individual terms.

ku.text: A geometric sequence has terms $u_n=u_1r^{n-1}$. The corresponding infinite series adds all these terms; its partial sum $S_n$ adds only the first $n$.
For a nonzero first term, the infinite geometric series converges if and only if $|r|<1$. In that case $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$.
The condition includes negative ratios between $-1$ and 0. Their terms alternate in sign but decrease in magnitude, and their partial sums approach a finite limit.
For $|r|<1$, $S_n=\dfrac{u_1(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ and $r^n\to0$, so $S_n\to\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$. A rounded partial sum can appear equal to the limit before it is exactly equal.
For $|r|<1$, the remainder after the first $n$ terms is $S_\infty-S_n=\dfrac{u_1r^n}{1-r}$, or equivalently the infinite sum beginning with $u_{n+1}$.
In a rebound-distance model, distinguish the initial fall from later upward and downward journeys. Whether a final downward journey is included depends on when the distance is measured.

misc.better: Use $|r|<1$. For example, $r=-2$ is less than 1 but a nonzero geometric series with that ratio diverges.

misc.weak: If the terms tend to zero, the partial sum must eventually stop changing.
misc.better: The partial sums can approach a limit while continuing to change. A rounded calculator display may hide those changes.
Here $r=-1/2$, so $|r|<1$ and the series converges to $8/(1+1/2)=16/3$.

misc.weak: The remainder after $n$ terms is the sum starting with $u_n$.
For a ball dropped from height $h$, total distance is just the sum of rebound heights.
misc.better: Include the initial fall, then count both upward and downward journeys for each rebound when the model continues until the ball comes to rest.

terms.text: Identify the ratio and test its magnitude against 1; explain why the condition is or is not satisfied.
State the first term and common ratio, verify $|r|<1$ and substitute into the infinite-sum formula.
Identify the first omitted term and sum the remaining geometric series, or subtract the partial sum from the infinite sum.

formula.text: For $r\ne1$, the finite geometric sum is $S_n=\dfrac{u_1(1-r^n)}{1-r}$.

worked.prompt: A ball is dropped from a height of 10 m. After each impact it rebounds to 60% of the height from which it fell. Assume this pattern continues indefinitely and ignore all other motion.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Find the sum of the first four rebound heights.
parts.a: The rebound heights form a geometric sequence with $u_1=6$ m and $r=0.6$. Thus $S_4=6(1-0.6^4)/(1-0.6)=13.056$ m.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Find the total distance travelled from release until the ball lands after its fourth rebound.
parts.a: Include the initial 10 m fall and both upward and downward legs for each of the first four rebounds: $10+2(13.056)=36.112$ m.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Find the limiting total distance travelled.
parts.a: Since $|0.6|<1$, the infinite sum of rebound heights is $6/(1-0.6)=15$ m. The total distance is $10+2(15)=40$ m.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Find the remaining distance after the landing described in part (b).

kq.q: Why can an infinite sum have a finite value?
kq.model: The finite partial sums can approach a limit. For a geometric series with $|r|<1$, the size of the remaining tail tends to zero.

kq.q: Why does a negative ratio not automatically mean divergence?
kq.model: A negative ratio alternates signs, but if its magnitude is less than 1, the terms shrink and the partial sums converge.

kq.q: Why is the first rebound not the original 10 m in the worked example?
kq.model: The original 10 m is the initial fall. The first rebound reaches 60% of it, or 6 m.

kq.q: Why are rebound heights doubled in the total-distance model?
kq.model: After each rebound, the ball travels up to that rebound height and then down by the same distance before the next impact.
